questions.prompt: A source drives a series resistor R, and the output is taken across a capacitor C to ground (the RC low-pass filter). What is its time constant \(\tau\)?
options: \(\tau=R/C\)
\(\tau=RC\)
\(\tau=R+C\)
questions.explanation: The governing equation is \(v_{o}=v_{s}-\tau\cdot dv_{o}/dt\) with \(\tau=RC\) (reader Eq. 1.2). Units: \(\Omega\cdot F=\) seconds. \(R/C\) and R + C do not have units of time, and \(1/(RC)\) is the corner (angular) frequency, not the time constant.

questions.prompt: A sinusoidal source with a very low frequency \((\omega\ll 1/RC)\) drives the RC low-pass filter (output across C). What does the output look like?
options: Almost the same as the input: about the same amplitude and nearly zero phase shift
Nearly zero amplitude, because the capacitor shorts the signal
Same amplitude but delayed by 90°
Twice the input amplitude
questions.explanation:
At low frequency the capacitor's current is tiny, so there is almost no voltage across R and \(v_{o}\approx v_{s}\): the signal passes undisturbed (reader Sec. 1.2.2).
• Near-zero output happens at HIGH frequency, where the capacitor shorts the signal.
• A 90° lag is the asymptotic phase at very HIGH frequency.
• A passive RC filter cannot amplify.

questions.prompt: An RC low-pass filter has \(R=10\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\) and \(C=10\ \mathrm{nF}\). What is its cutoff (−3 dB) frequency \(f_{c}=1/(2\pi RC)\)?
questions.explanation:
\(\tau=RC=10\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\times 10\ \mathrm{nF}=100\ \mu\mathrm{s}\). \(\omega_{c}=1/\tau=10{,}000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\), so \(f_{c}=\omega_{c}/(2\pi)=10{,}000/6.2832=1592\ \mathrm{Hz}\).
Common mistake: quoting \(1/\tau=10{,}000\) as Hz; that is \(\mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\). You must divide by \(2\pi\).

questions.prompt: An RC low-pass filter has \(R=2\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\) and \(C=500\ \mathrm{nF}\). The capacitor starts discharged, and at \(t=0\) the source steps from 0 V to 5 V. What is \(v_{o}\) at \(t=2\ \mathrm{ms}\)?
questions.explanation:
\(\tau=RC=2\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\times 500\ \mathrm{nF}=1\ \mathrm{ms}\). Step response: \(v_{o}(t)=V_{s}(1-e^{-t/\tau})\).
At \(t=2\ \mathrm{ms}=2\tau\): \(v_{o}=5(1-e^{-2})=5(1-0.1353)=4.323\ \mathrm{V}\).
Common mistakes: \(5e^{-2}=0.68\ \mathrm{V}\) (using the decay instead of the rise), or \(5(1-e^{-1})=3.16\ \mathrm{V}\) (using \(t=\tau\)).

questions.prompt: An RC low-pass filter has \(\tau=RC=100\ \mu\mathrm{s}\). It is driven by \(v_{s}=3\cos(\omega t)\) volts with \(\omega=20\ \mathrm{krad}/\mathrm{s}\). What is the steady-state amplitude of \(v_{o}\)?
questions.explanation:
\(\omega\tau=20{,}000\times 100\ \mu\mathrm{s}=2\). Amplitude response: \(|V_{o}/V_{s}|=1/\sqrt{1+(\omega\tau)^{2}}=1/\sqrt{5}=0.4472\).
Output amplitude \(=3\ \mathrm{V}\times 0.4472=1.342\ \mathrm{V}\) (and the phase is \(-\tan^{-1}(2)=-63.4^{\circ}\)).
Common mistake: using \(1/(1+\omega\tau)=1/3\) (forgetting the square root of the sum of squares), which gives 1.0 V.

questions.prompt: An RC low-pass filter is driven by a sinusoid whose angular frequency is exactly \(\omega=1/\tau\). Compared with the input, the steady-state output has…
options: amplitude \(0.5\times\) input and a phase lag of 45°
amplitude \(0.707\times\) input and a phase LEAD of 45°
amplitude \(0.707\times\) input and a phase lag of 90°
amplitude \(0.707\times\) input and a phase lag of 45°
questions.explanation:
With \(\omega\tau=1\): \(|H|=1/\sqrt{1+1}=0.707\ (-3\ \mathrm{dB}\), half the power) and \(\angle H=-\tan^{-1}(1)=-45^{\circ}\) (a lag).
• 0.5 is the magnitude of a half-voltage point, not the −3 dB point.
• The low-pass output lags the input; a lead would be for a high-pass.
• 90° lag is only reached asymptotically at very high frequency.
questions.figure_alt: Bode magnitude of the RC low-pass: flat, then falling 20 dB per decade beyond the corner at omega = 1/tau; the exact curve is dashed.

questions.prompt: The RC low-pass filter starts with the capacitor uncharged \((v_{o}(0)=0)\). At \(t=0\), a source \(v_{s}=V_{s}\ \cos(\omega t)\) is connected. Which description of \(v_{o}(t)\) for \(t\ge 0\) is correct?
options: \(v_{o}(t)\) is exactly the steady-state sinusoid \(|H|V_{s}\ \cos(\omega t+\phi)\) for all \(t\ge 0\), since the input is a sinusoid
\(v_{o}(t)=\) steady-state sinusoid + a transient that decays with time constant \(1/\omega\)
\(v_{o}(t)=\) steady-state sinusoid + a decaying transient \(K\cdot e^{-t/\tau}\), with K chosen so that \(v_{o}(0)=0\)
\(v_{o}(t)=\) steady-state sinusoid + a sinusoidal transient at frequency \(1/\tau\) that never decays
questions.explanation:
The \(ODE\ v_{o}+\tau\ dv_{o}/dt=v_{s}\) has a particular solution (the sinusoidal steady state) plus a homogeneous solution \(K\cdot e^{-t/\tau}\) that depends on the filter, not the source. The initial condition \(v_{o}(0)=0\) fixes \(K=\) −(steady-state value at \(t=0\)).
• The pure sinusoid would have \(v_{o}(0)=|H|V_{s}\ \cos \phi\ne 0\), which would require the capacitor voltage to jump (impossible).
• The transient's time constant is \(\tau=RC\), a property of the circuit, not \(1/\omega\).
• The homogeneous solution is a real decaying exponential, not an undamped oscillation.
This is why the complex-exponential method gives only the steady state.
questions.figure_alt: The source cosine (dashed) and the capacitor voltage, which starts at zero and settles into a sinusoid.

questions.prompt: An RC low-pass filter has \(R=10\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\) and \(C=1\ \mathrm{nF}\). A step is applied and the output rises toward its final value. What is the 10%–90% rise time of the output?
questions.explanation:
\(\tau=RC=10\ \mu\mathrm{s}\). The step response is \(v_{o}=V_{f}(1-e^{-t/\tau})\).
10% point: \(t_{10}=-\tau\ \ln(0.9)=1.054\ \mu\mathrm{s}\). 90% point: \(t_{90}=-\tau\ \ln(0.1)=23.03\ \mu\mathrm{s}\).
Rise time \(=t_{90}-t_{10}=\tau\ \ln 9=2.197\tau=21.97\ \mu\mathrm{s}\).
Common mistakes: answering \(\tau=10\ \mu\mathrm{s}\) (that is the 63% time), or \(t_{90}=2.303\tau=23.0\ \mu\mathrm{s}\) (measured from \(t=0\) rather than from the 10% point).
questions.figure_alt: Rising exponential step response with dashed lines at 10 percent and 90 percent of the final value.

questions.prompt: An RC low-pass filter (\(R=1\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\), \(C=1\ \mu\mathrm{F}\)) now has a load resistor \(R_{L}=1\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\) connected in parallel with C. The capacitor starts discharged and a 10 V step is applied. What are the final output voltage and the time constant?
options: Final value 10 V, time constant 1 ms
Final value 5 V, time constant 0.5 ms
Final value 5 V, time constant 1 ms
Final value 10 V, time constant 0.5 ms
questions.explanation:
At DC the capacitor is an open circuit, so R and \(R_{L}\) form a divider: \(V_{\mathrm{final}}=10\times 1k/(1k+1k)=5\ \mathrm{V}\) (the load drains current, so the output no longer reaches 10 V).
The resistance seen by the capacitor (source shorted) is \(R\parallel R_{L}=500\ \Omega\), so \(\tau=(R\parallel R_{L})C=500\ \Omega\times 1\ \mu\mathrm{F}=0.5\ \mathrm{ms}\).
• '10 V, 1 ms' ignores the load completely.
• '5 V, 1 ms' gets the divider but uses R instead of \(R\parallel R_{L}\).
• '10 V, 0.5 ms' gets the faster \(\tau\) but misses the divider.

questions.prompt: Preview of sinusoidal steady state. A later skill shows that replacing \(d/dt\) by \(j\omega\) in the RC filter equation gives \(H(j\omega)=V_{o}/V_{s}=1/(1+j\omega RC)\). Take \(R=1\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\), \(C=159\ \mathrm{nF}\) and a source \(2\cos(2\pi\cdot 1000\cdot t)\ \mathrm{V}\). What is the steady-state amplitude of \(v_{o}\)?
questions.explanation:
\(\tau=RC=1\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\times 159\ \mathrm{nF}=159\ \mu\mathrm{s}\). \(\omega=2\pi\cdot 1000=6283\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\), so \(\omega\tau=0.999\approx 1\).
\(|H|=1/\sqrt{1+(\omega\tau)^{2}}=0.7075\), so the amplitude is \(2\times 0.7075=1.415\ \mathrm{V}\).
The phase is \(\angle H=-\tan^{-1}(\omega\tau)=-44.97^{\circ}\approx-45^{\circ}\): this is the 'corner frequency' case \((f_{c}=1/(2\pi RC)\approx 1\ \mathrm{kHz})\).

questions.prompt: Preview of step response. A later skill uses the step response to measure delay. For an RC low-pass filter with \(R=2.2\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\) and \(C=10\ \mathrm{nF}\), the output is \(v_{o}=V_{f}(1-e^{-t/RC})\) after a step. How long does the output take to reach 50% of its final value?
questions.explanation:
Set \(1-e^{-t/\tau}=0.5\) ⇒ \(e^{-t/\tau}=0.5\) ⇒ \(t=\tau\ \ln 2=0.693\tau\).
\(\tau=RC=2.2\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\times 10\ \mathrm{nF}=22\ \mu\mathrm{s}\), so \(t_{50}=0.693\times 22\ \mu\mathrm{s}=15.25\ \mu\mathrm{s}\).
Common mistake: using \(t=\tau\) (that is the 63.2% point).
questions.figure_alt: Normalized RC step response with a dashed line at 50 percent of the final value.

questions.prompt: Preview of Bode plots. A later skill plots |H| in decibels, \(\mathrm{dB}=20\cdot\log_{10}|V_{o}/V_{s}|\). You want an RC low-pass filter to attenuate a 10 kHz tone by 20 dB (output amplitude \(=0.1\times\) input). Using \(|H|=1/\sqrt{1+(\omega\tau)^{2}}\), what time constant \(\tau=RC\) is required?
questions.explanation:
−20 dB means \(|H|=10^{-20/20}=0.1\).
\(1/\sqrt{1+(\omega\tau)^{2}}=0.1\) ⇒ \(1+(\omega\tau)^{2}=100\) ⇒ \(\omega\tau=\sqrt{99}=9.95\).
\(\omega=2\pi\times 10\ \mathrm{kHz}=62{,}832\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\) ⇒ \(\tau=9.95/62{,}832=158.4\ \mu\mathrm{s}\).
Common mistake: using the high-frequency approximation \(\omega\tau\approx 10\), which gives \(\tau=159.2\ \mu\mathrm{s}\); it is within 0.5%, but the exact relation includes the '1 +' term.
